en: Bhāvamiśra: Bhāvaprakāśa;
Bhāvaprakāśa, Vargaprakaraṇa.
The Aśvins spoke these words to Dakṣa Prajāpati, who was seated among the group beginning with Harītakī:
"From where was the Harītakī born, and how many varieties does it have? (1)
How many rasas are enumerated, and how many uparasas are traditionally taught?
How many names have been mentioned, and what is their characteristic?
What are their colors, what are their qualities, and which one is employed where?
"With what substance is it conjoined, and which diseases does it dispel?
O Blessed One, you should explain this question exactly as it has been asked.
Having heard the words of the two Aśvins, Dakṣa spoke these words:
As Śakra was drinking the nectar, a drop fell upon the earth;
from that divine [drop] there arose the *harītakī*, which has seven births.
It is known as *harītakī*, *abhayā*, *pathyā*, *kāyasthā*, *pūtanā*, and *amṛtā*.
Haimavatī, avyathā, cetakī, śreyasī, and śivā; also vayaḥsthā, vijayā, jīvantī, and rohiṇī;
as well as vijayā, rohiṇī, pūtanā, amṛtā, and abhayā.
Jīvantī and Cetakī—these are the seven varieties of Pathyā (Harītakī).
Vijayā is found on the Vindhya mountains; Cetakī originates from the Himālayas; Pūtanā is found in Sindh; Rohiṇī is said to be born in Pratiṣṭhāna;
Amṛtā and Abhayā are produced in the land called Surāṣṭra; and Jīvantī is likewise mentioned. Thus, the wise declare that there are seven distinct types of Harītakī.

Vijayā is known by the shape of a bottle-gourd; that which is round is remembered as Rohiṇī. Pūtanā is thin and bony, while Amṛtā is said to be fleshy. Abhayā is described as having five lines, and Jīvantī is golden-colored.
The three-lined variety is known as *cetakī*; this is the form of the seven [types of harītakī].
*Vijayā* is used for all diseases; *rohiṇī* is for healing wounds.
*Pūtanā* should be employed as a paste, while *amṛtā* is beneficial for purification.
Abhayā is recommended for eye diseases, and jīvantī removes all diseases.
For the purpose of making a powder, cetakī is recommended; one should employ it according to the specific application.
Cetakī is said to be of two kinds according to its color: white and black.
The white [line] is known to be six finger-breadths long, while the black one is one finger-breadth;
some [the goddess Śivā] would distinguish [the disciple] by the mere taste, some by the scent, some by touch, and another by sight—thus she distinguishes in four ways. (14–15)
Those men, as well as cattle, birds, wild animals, and the like, who approach the shade of the *cetakī* tree, are split asunder at that very moment. Indeed,
as long as the *cetakī* is held in the hand of a living being, [it remains so].
It may indeed be broken up by its own force through its potency; of this there is no doubt.
For kings who are delicate, emaciated, and averse to medicine, *cetakī* is highly recommended—it is beneficial and provides a pleasant purgation. // 17–18 //

Among the seven types of *jāti*, *vijayā* is considered the foremost; it is easy to administer, easily obtained, and recommended for all diseases. *Harītakī* possesses five tastes, is slightly salty, and is most excellent. (19)
It is dry, hot, digestive, intellect-promoting, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and an elixir (rasāyana).
It is beneficial for the eyes, light, life-prolonging, nourishing, and carminative.
It cures asthma, cough, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, edema, abdominal enlargements, and worms.
It cures disorders of voice, diseases of the digestive tract,

constipation, and irregular fevers; as well as abdominal tumors, flatulence, thirst, vomiting, hiccups, itching, heart disease, jaundice, colic, abdominal distension, splenic enlargement, and liver disease.
It destroys urinary calculi, dysuria, and urinary obstruction.
Because it is sweet, bitter, and astringent, it removes pitta;
because it is pungent, bitter, and astringent, and due to its acidity, the auspicious *śivā* (harītakī) removes kapha and vāta.
Since harītakī (śivā) possesses pungent and sour tastes, it produces pitta; why then does it not produce vāta? [The answer is:

Its capacity to destroy the doṣas is established through its specific potency (prabhāva), which is now being elucidated through logical reasons for the sake of the student's understanding; nothing new is being created here.

The difference in function and the equality in quality [of a single substance] are observed due to the distinction of their substrates; therefore, one should not conclude that they are not distinct, just as in the case of the jackfruit (*dhātrī*) and the *lakuca* fruit.
For instance, sweetness resides in the marrow of the *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan), while acidity is established in its fiber.
The juice is bitter in the stalk, pungent in the skin, and astringent when residing in the pith;
it is unctuous, dense, round, and heavy. That which sinks when cast into water is excellent and, as described, bestows superlative qualities.

When the fruit of the *harītakī* possesses the nine qualities and so forth, and likewise when two *karṣas* [of weight] are found in a single fruit—where both these conditions exist, it is called the best.
When chewed, it increases the digestive fire; when ground into a paste, it purifies the waste.
Haritaki, when steamed, is astringent and wholesome; when fried, it is said to alleviate the three doṣas.
Taken with food, Haritaki awakens the intellect, strength, and the senses; it eradicates pitta, kapha, and vāta; and it causes the discharge of urine, feces, and impurities. (30–31)
Harītakī, when administered after a meal, quickly removes the disorders caused by food and drink, as well as those arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha;
with salt it destroys kapha, and with sugar it destroys pitta.
With ghee, it cures diseases born of wind (vāta); with jaggery, it cures all diseases.

One who desires the qualities of an elixir (rasāyana) should consume Abhayā in sequence with rock salt, sugar, ginger, Pippalī, honey, and jaggery during the rainy season and the other seasons respectively.
One who is exhausted by travel, devoid of strength, coarse, emaciated, or weakened by fasting;
one with a predominance of *pitta*, a pregnant woman, and one who has lost blood—these should not eat *abhayā*.
*Vibhītaka* is known as *triliṅga* and *akṣa*; it is also called *karṣaphala*.
The Vibhītaka tree is known as Kalidruma, Bhūtavāsa, and Kaliyugālaya.
It has a sweet post-digestive effect (pāka), is astringent (kaṣāya), and alleviates phlegm and bile.
It is hot in potency (uṣṇavīrya) but cold to the touch (himasparśa); it is a laxative and destroys cough.
The kernel of the *vibhītaka* is parched, beneficial for the eyes, good for the hair, and destroys worms and discoloration;
it removes thirst, vomiting, phlegm, and wind, and is light.
It is astringent and intoxicating. Furthermore, the kernel of the *dhātrī* possesses these same qualities.
Āmalaka is declared to be of three types: dhātrī, tiṣyaphalā, and amṛtā.
The dhātrī fruit is equal to harītakī, but it is especially distinguished as a supreme remedy for hemorrhaging and urinary disorders, an aphrodisiac, and an elixir of life (rasāyana).
The fruit of the dhātrī (myrobalan) conquers the three doṣas: it subdues vāta due to its acidity, pitta due to its sweetness and coolness, and kapha due to its dryness and astringency.
Whatever kind of potency each particular fruit possesses in this world, [it acts accordingly].
One should prescribe even the marrow with the same respective potency.
[42] From the fruits of *pathyā*, *vibhīta*, and *dhātrī*, there is *triphalā*; it is equal to the three fruits.
This *phalatrika* is known as *triphalā*, and it is also celebrated as *varā*. [43]

Triphalā destroys kapha and pitta, cures urinary disorders and skin diseases, is laxative, beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, improves appetite, and destroys irregular fevers. Śuṇṭhī, viśvā, and viśva are synonyms for nāgara and viśvabheṣaja.
Ūṣaṇa, kaṭubhadra, śṛṅgavera, and mahauṣadha—these are synonyms for śuṇṭhī (dry ginger).
It is appetizing, destroys wind-disorders, promotes digestion, is pungent, and light.
It is unctuous, hot, and sweet in its post-digestive effect; it removes obstructions caused by phlegm and wind.

It is aphrodisiac and beneficial for the voice; it destroys vomiting, dyspnea, colic, cough, and heart disease, as well as elephantiasis, edema, hemorrhoids, flatulence, abdominal enlargement, and wind disorders (47).
This is because it abounds in fiery qualities and dries up the watery element.
That which collects impurity is indeed "grasping" (grāhin), just like ginger and other such substances. But how could that which breaks up obstructions be considered "grasping"?
For its capacity lies in breaking up obstructions, not in the falling away of impurity.
Ārdraka, śṛṅgavera, kaṭubhadra, and likewise ārdrikā are synonyms.
Ārdrikā is considered to be laxative, heavy, sharp, hot, and digestive.
It is pungent, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), dry, and it removes wind and phlegm.
All those qualities that have been described for ginger are also present in full in fresh ginger (ārdraka).
Eating salted fresh ginger at the beginning of a meal is always wholesome;
it stimulates the digestive fire, improves the appetite, and cleanses the tongue and throat.

Fresh ginger (ārdraka) is not at all recommended in cases of skin diseases, impotence, difficult urination, internal hemorrhaging, ulcers, or fever; nor during the heat of summer or the autumn season.
Pippalī, māgadhī, kṛṣṇā, vaidehī, capalā, and kaṇā are synonyms for long pepper.
Upakulyā, uṣaṇā, śauṇḍī, kolā, and tīkṣṇataṇḍulā are synonyms for pippalī. It is digestive, aphrodisiac, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and a rejuvenative elixir.
It is not hot, pungent, unctuous, light, and it alleviates vāta and kapha.
Pippalī is purgative and destroys asthma,

cough, abdominal enlargement, fever, skin diseases, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, colic, undigested toxins (āmam), and wind disorders. When fresh, it increases phlegm (kapha) and is unctuous, cooling, sweet, and heavy.
When dried, it pacifies bile, but when fresh, it aggravates bile.
Pippalī combined with honey destroys fat and phlegm;
it removes dyspnea, cough, and fever, and is aphrodisiac, intellect-promoting, and increases the digestive fire.
Guda-pippalī (long pepper with jaggery) is recommended for chronic fever and weak digestion;
it cures cough, indigestion, anorexia, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, and worm infestations.
In this preparation, the physicians maintain that the jaggery should be double the amount of the long pepper powder. (59)
Marica, vellaja, kṛṣṇa, ūṣaṇa, and dharmapattana are synonyms for black pepper.
Black pepper is pungent, sharp, digestive, and conquers phlegm and wind;
it is hot, increases bile, is dry, and removes asthma, colic, and worms.
It is moist, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), not excessively hot, pungent, heavy, slightly sharp in quality, causes salivation, and does not increase bile (apittala). 62.
The three—ginger (viśva), long pepper (upakulyā), and black pepper (marica)—are called trikaṭu.

The three pungents (kaṭutrikam) are called trikaṭu, tryūṣaṇa, and vyoṣa. Tryūṣaṇa stimulates digestion and cures asthma, cough, skin diseases, abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary disorders (meha), phlegm-related ailments, obesity, fat-related disorders, elephantiasis (ślīpada), and chronic catarrh (pīnasa).
Granthika, pippalīmūla, ūṣaṇa, and caṭakāśiras are digestive stimulants;
pippalīmūla is pungent, hot, a digestive aid,
light, dry, increases pitta, is a purgative, and cures kapha and vāta disorders of the abdomen.
It destroys abdominal distension, splenic disorders, and tumors, and removes worms, dyspnea, and consumption.
Tryūṣaṇa (the three pungents) along with kaṇāmūla is called Caturūṣaṇa;
the qualities of Vyoṣa are said to be present in Caturūṣaṇa, but with an increase [in potency].
Cavya is indeed *cavikā*, and it is likewise described as hot (*uṣṇā*).
Cavya possesses the qualities of *kaṇāmūla* (black pepper root), and it specifically destroys hemorrhoids (*gudaja*).
The fruit of *cavikā* is called *gajapippalī* by the wise.
Kapivallī, kolavallī, śreyasī, and that which is vaśira;
as well as gajakṛṣṇā—these are pungent, they remove vāta and kapha, increase the digestive fire, are hot in potency, and destroy diarrhea, dyspnea, diseases of the throat, and worms. (69–70)
Citraka is also known as anala, pīṭha, vyāla, and uṣaṇa.
Citraka is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), stimulates the digestive fire, is appetizing, and light.
It is dry and hot; it cures disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema, hemorrhoids, worms, and cough.
It alleviates vāta and kapha, is astringent, subdues vāta, and removes kapha and pitta.
(72) Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara—these five, when taken in the measure of a kola each, are called pañcakola. (73)
Pañcakola is pungent in taste and digestion; it is considered to stimulate the appetite.
It is sharp and hot, an excellent digestive aid, a stimulant of the digestive fire, and a subduer of phlegm and wind.
It destroys abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, flatulence, and colic, though it provokes bile. (74)
The five-spices group (pañcakola), together with black pepper, is declared to be the "six pungents" (ṣaḍūṣaṇa).
It possesses the qualities of the five-spices group; moreover, it is dry, hot, and destroys poison. Yavānī, ugragandhā, brahmadarbhā, and ajamodikā [constitute the next group]. 75–76.
That same [plant] is called dīpyakā, dīpyā, and likewise yavasāhvayā;
it is yavānī. It is digestive, appetizing, sharp, hot, pungent, and light.
It is also a stimulant of digestion, bitter, increases bile, and removes seminal pain.
It cures abdominal enlargement due to wind and phlegm, flatulence, gulma, splenic disorders, and worms.
Ajamodā, kharāśvā, māyūrī, dīpyaka, as well as brahmakuśā, kāravī, and locamastakā are thus described. (78–79)
Ajamodā is pungent and sharp, a digestive stimulant, and it subdues phlegm and wind.
It is hot, causes a burning sensation, is pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, strength-promoting, and light.
It removes eye diseases, worms, vomiting, hiccup, and pain from enemas. (80)
Pārasīkayavānī is similar to yavānī in its qualities;
it is specifically digestive, appetizing, astringent, intoxicating, and heavy.
Jīraka is jaraṇa and ajājī; kaṇā is dīrghajīraka. (81–82)
Black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīra*) is fragrant and likewise purifies the eructation;
it is also called *kālājājī*, *suṣavī*, *kālikā*, and *upakālikā*.
*Pṛthvīkā* and *kāravī* are synonyms for *pṛthvī*; it is also known as *pṛthukṛṣṇā* and *upakuñcikā*.
Upakuñcī, kuñcī, and also bṛhajjīraka—
this triad of cumin is dry, pungent, hot, digestive, and light; it is astringent, increases bile, promotes intelligence, and purifies the uterus.

Coriander (dhānyaka) destroys fever, is purifying, aphrodisiac, strengthening, appetizing, and removes phlegm; it is beneficial for the eyes and cures wind-disorders, flatulence, abdominal tumors, vomiting, and diarrhea. It is also known as dhānaka, dhānya, dhānā, and dhāneyaka.
Kunaṭī, dhenukā, chattrā, kustumburu,
vitunnaka, dhānyaka, and tuvara are unctuous, non-aphrodisiac, diuretic, and light.
They are known to be bitter, pungent, hot in potency, digestive stimulants, and carminatives.
It destroys fever, improves appetite, is astringent, sweet in digestion, and alleviates the three doṣas;
it removes thirst, burning sensations, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, emaciation, and worms.
When fresh, it possesses these same qualities, is sweet, and specifically destroys pitta. (89)
Śatapuṣpā, śatāhvā, madhurā, kāravī, misi, atilambī, sitacchattrā, and saṃhitacchattrikā;
also chattrā, śāleya, śālīna, miśreyā, madhurā, and misi.
Śatapuṣpā is light, sharp, increases pitta, stimulates digestion, and is pungent.
It is hot and removes fever, wind, phlegm, wounds, colic, and eye diseases.
Miśreyā is said to possess those same qualities, with the specific distinction that it cures vaginal pain.
Methikā, methinī, methī, dīpanī, and bahupattrikā alleviate sluggish digestion, are beneficial for the heart, and remove constipation, worms, and seminal disorders.
They are dry and hot, act as digestive stimulants, and cure cough, vomiting, phlegm, and wind.
(93) Methikā, methinī, methī, dīpanī, bahupattrikā.
Bodhinī, Bahubījā, Jyotirgandhaphalā;
likewise Vallarī, Cakrikā, Manthā, Miśrapuṣpā, Kairavī, Kuñcikā, Bahuparṇī, Pītabījā, and Municchadā. // 94–95 //

Methikā pacifies wind, destroys phlegm, and cures fever; however, the wild variety possesses slightly fewer qualities, yet it is highly esteemed for horses. Candrikā removes skin diseases and causes urinary disorders in cattle.
Nandinī, kāravī, bhadrā, vāsapuṣpā, and suvāsarā—these are known as candraśūra. They are beneficial for those suffering from hiccups, wind-disorders, phlegm, and diarrhea;
they counteract diseases of blood and wind, and increase strength and nourishment.
Methikā, candraśūra, kālājājī, and yavānikā—
this group of four is known as the "four seeds.
When this powder is consumed daily, it destroys diseases of the wind (vāta).
It cures indigestion, colic, flatulence, pain in the flanks, and distress in the waist.
*Sahasravedhin*, *jatuka*, *vāhlīka*, *hiṅgu*, and *rāmaṭha*—these are synonyms for asafoetida.
Asafoetida is hot, digestive, appetizing, sharp, and it overcomes wind and stiffness.
It destroys colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, and worms, and increases pitta.
Vacā, ugragandhā, ṣaḍgranthā, golomī, śataparvikā, kṣudrapattrī, maṅgalyā, jaṭilā, ugrā, and lomaśā are synonyms for vacā. (102–103)

Vacā has a pungent odor; it is acrid, bitter, and hot. It induces vomiting, stimulates the digestive fire, and destroys constipation, flatulence, and colic. It purifies the feces and urine and removes epilepsy, phlegm, insanity, and disorders caused by spirits, insects, and wind. (104)
The white variety from Persia is called *haimavatī*;
likewise, that which is declared to be from the Himalayas specifically destroys wind (*vāta*).
It is both fragrant and pungent-smelling, and it especially cures phlegm and cough.
It produces a beautiful voice, is palatable, and cleanses the heart, throat, and mouth.
The *sthūlagranthi* variety is fragrant, but it is considered to have inferior qualities compared to the former.
The *vacā* from another continent is slightly bitter and hot, and it stimulates the digestive fire.
It destroys constipation, flatulence, and colic; it purifies the feces and urine.
It specifically dispels wind diseases, epilepsy, insanity, and bodily pain, and is a destroyer of syphilis (phiraṅga). // 108–109 //
Havuṣā is known as vapuṣā, visrā, and parāśvatthaphalā;
it is called matsyagandhā, plīhahantrī, viṣaghnī, and dhvāṅkṣanāśinī.
(110) Havuṣā stimulates digestion, is bitter, mild, hot, astringent, and heavy.
It removes bile-disorders, abdominal enlargements, wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), and colic;
another variety is said to possess these same qualities, though there is a difference in form between the two.
Viḍaṅga is masculine or neuter; it is the destroyer of worms and the annihilator of living parasites.
Rice, as well as vellam, amoghā, and citrataṇḍulā;
viḍaṅga is pungent, sharp, hot, dry, digestive, and light;
it cures colic, flatulence, abdominal disorders, phlegm, worms, and the obstruction of vāta.
Tumburu is known as saurabha, saura, vanaja, sānuja, and andhaka.
Tumburu is celebrated for its bitterness; it is pungent even in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
It is dry, hot, digestive-stimulant (dīpana), sharp, appetizing, light, and causes a burning sensation (vidāhin).

It destroys diseases of the wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), ailments of the eyes, ears, lips, and head, heaviness of the body, worms, leprosy (kuṣṭha), colic (śūla), loss of appetite (aruci), asthma (śvāsa), splenic disorders (plīha), and dysuria (kṛcchra).
It is known as vaṃśarocanā, vāṃśī, tugākṣīrī, tugā, and śubhā.
Tvakkṣīrī, vaṃśajā, śubhrā, vaṃśakṣīrī, and vaiṇavī are synonyms for bamboo-milk.
It is nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, sweet, and cooling;
it cures thirst, cough, fever, asthma, consumption, hemorrhaging, and jaundice.
The decoctions [of these] cure skin diseases (kuṣṭha), ulcers, and anemia, and they overcome Vāta and urinary distress. Samudraphena, phena, ḍiṇḍīra, and likewise abdhikapha—
samudraphena is beneficial for the eyes, scraping, and cooling.
The *kaṣāya* (decoction) destroys poison and bile, removes earache and *kapha*, and is laxative.
*Jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, the two *medās*, the two *kākolīs*, *ṛddhi*, and *vṛddhi*—these eight substances constitute the "Group of Eight" (*aṣṭavarga*) as described by Caraka and others. (120–121)

The group of eight [fruits] is cooling, sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and heavy; it promotes the healing of fractures, increases sexual desire, strength, and vigor, and cures disorders of wind (vāta), blood (asṛj), thirst, burning sensations, fever, urinary disorders (meha), and consumption (kṣaya). 122
Jīvaka and Ṛṣabhaka are known to originate from the peaks of the Himālaya mountains;
their bulbs are like those of garlic (rasona), being pithless and possessing fine leaves. Jīvaka is shaped like a brush (kūrcaka), while Ṛṣabha resembles the horn of a bull.
Jīvaka, Madhura, Śṛṅga, Hrasvāṅga, Kūrcaśīrṣaka, Ṛṣabha,
Vṛṣabha, Dhīra, Viṣāṇin, and Drākṣa— these are synonyms for Jīvaka and Ṛṣabhaka. They are strengthening, cooling, and increase semen and phlegm.
Sweet, they remove bile, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, emaciation, wind disorders, and consumption.
The tuber known as Mahāmedā grows in regions such as Moraṅga;
the lords of sages have stated that Mahāmedā is also called Khanīmedā.
The bulbous root known as Mahāmedā resembles a fresh ginger root; it grows on a creeper and is very pale white. Its characteristics are now described:
the white bulb should be cut with a fingernail, and it should exude a substance resembling the bodily element of fat (medas).
That which is known as *medā* should be recognized by people intent on inquiry [as follows]:
*śalyaparṇī*, *maṇicchidrā*, *medā*, *medobhavā*, *adhvarā*, *mahāmedā*, *vasucchidrā*, *tridantī*, and *devatāmaṇi*. (129–130)

Medā-yuga (the pair of Medās) is heavy, sweet, aphrodisiac, increases breast milk and phlegm, is nourishing, cooling, and cures pitta, blood disorders, vāta, and fever. Kṣīrakākolī grows in the same place where Mahāmedā is found. 131–132.
Where *kākolī* is found, there *kṣīrakākolī* is produced;
its bulb is like that of *pīvarī*, milky, and possessed of a pleasant fragrance.
That is called *kṣīrakākolī*; the characteristics of *kākolī* are now described.
Just as there is *kṣīrakākolī*, so too there may be *kākoly*. This one may be somewhat black; this is the distinction between the two.
*Kākolī* is also called *vāyasolī*, and likewise *vīrā* and *kāyasthikā*.
That white variety is *kṣīrakākolī*, *vayaḥsthā*, *kṣīravallikā*, *kathitā*, *kṣīriṇī*, *dhīrā*, *kṣīraśuklā*, and *payasvinī*.
The pair of *kākolī*s is cooling, semen-fortifying, sweet, and heavy.
It is nourishing and removes wind, burning sensations, hemorrhagic disorders, consumption, and fever.
(137) There are two tubers, Ṛddhi and Vṛddhi, found in the Kośala region on the mountain;
the tuber is covered with white hair, grows from a creeper, and is perforated by holes. (138)
That very [practice] is both *ṛddhi* (prosperity) and *vṛddhi* (growth); I shall now describe the distinction between these two.
*Ṛddhi* is like a knot of cotton, and its fruit is a counter-clockwise rotation;
whereas *vṛddhi* is said by the great seers to have the fruit of a clockwise rotation.
*Ṛddhi*, *yogya*, *siddhi*, and *lakṣmī* are also names for *vṛddhi*.
(140) *Ṛddhi* is strengthening, alleviates the three *doṣas*, increases semen, is sweet, and heavy;
it bestows vitality and sovereignty, and destroys fainting and *raktapitta*. (141)
Vṛddhi is known to be cooling, nourishing, and sweet;
it is aphrodisiac, pacifies pitta and blood disorders, and removes chest wounds, coughs, and consumption.
(142) This group of eight is exceedingly rare even for kings.
Therefore, the physician should take a substitute for this that possesses its qualities;
a substitute should be similar to the primary substance.
Even when both pairs—medā and jīvaka, and kākolī and ṛddhi—are unavailable, [one should still proceed].
One should sequentially add *varī*, *vidārī*, *aśvagandhā*, and *vārāhī*;
in place of *medā* and *mahāmedā*, one should use the root of *śatāvarī*; and in place of *jīvaka* and *ṛṣabhaka*, one should use the root of *vidārī*.
In place of *kākolī* and *kṣīrakākolī*, one should add the root of *aśvagandhā*;
in place of *ṛddhi* and *vṛddhi*, one should add the tuber of *vārāhī*, which is equal to them in its qualities.
Likewise, [one should add] *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and *klītaka*.
The other variety is *klītanaka*, which is called *madhūlikā* when found in water.
Yaṣṭī is cooling, heavy, sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and promotes strength and complexion;
it is very unctuous, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the hair, good for the voice, and subdues pitta, vāta, and blood disorders.
It removes ulcers, swelling, poison, vomiting, thirst, exhaustion, and wasting.
Kāmpilla is also known as karkaśa, candra, raktāṅga, and rocana.
Kāmpilla [cures] disorders of kapha, pitta, blood, worms, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and ulcers.
The *recī* (purgative) variety is pungent and hot; it destroys urinary disorders (*meha*), abdominal distension (*ānāha*), poison, and stones.
*Āragvadha*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śamyāka*, *caturaṅgula*, *ārevata*, *vyādhighāta*, *kṛtamāla*, and *suvarṇaka* are synonyms for this plant. (147–148)
Karṇikāra, Dīrghaphala, Svarṇāṅga, and Svarṇabhūṣaṇa are synonyms for Āragvadha. It is heavy, sweet, cooling, and the best among purgatives;
it cures fever, heart disease, hemorrhaging from pitta, vāta disorders, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and colic.
Its fruit is laxative, appetizing, and removes skin diseases (kuṣṭha), pitta, and kapha.
It is always wholesome in cases of fever and is an excellent cleanser of the digestive tract (koṣṭha).
Kaṭvī, however, is known as kaṭukā, tiktā, kṛṣṇabhedā, and kaṭaṃbharā.
Aśokā, matsyaśakalā, cakrāṅgī, and śakulādanī;
matsyapittā, kāṇḍaruhā, rohiṇī, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Kaṭvī, however, is known as kaṭukā; it is bitter in its post-digestive effect (pāka), pungent, astringent, cold, and light. // 152–153 //

Kirātatikta (Chiretta) is purgative, digestive-stimulant, and pleasant for the heart; it removes phlegm, bile, and fever, and it destroys urinary disorders, asthma, cough, hemorrhaging, burning sensations, skin diseases, and worms. It is also known as Kairāta, Kaṭutikta, and Kirātaka. (154–155)
*Kāṇḍatikta*, *anāryatikta*, *bhūnimba*, and *rāmasenaka* are synonyms for one type of *kirāta*.
Another is *naipāla*, which is half-bitter (*ardhatikta*) and a destroyer of fever (*jvarāntaka*).
*Kirāta* is *sāraka*, parching (*rūkṣa*), cooling (*śītala*), bitter (*tikta*), and light (*laghu*).
It cures fever arising from the combination of humors (saṃnipātajvara), dyspnea, phlegm, bile, blood, and burning sensations;
it also removes cough, swelling, thirst, leprosy, fever, ulcers, and worms.
Thus have been described *kuṭaja* seeds, as well as *yava* and *indrayava*.
There is also kaliṅga and kāliṅga, as well as bhadrayava.
In some places, the very name of Indra serves as its designation;
its fruits are called indrayavas, and likewise bhadrayavas.
Indrayava destroys the three doṣas, is astringent, pungent, and cold;

it cures fever, diarrhea, hemorrhoidal bleeding, vomiting, erysipelas, and skin diseases. It stimulates digestion and overcomes hemorrhoids, blood disorders, vāta-blood disorders, phlegm, and colic. (160–161)
Madana, chardana, piṇḍa, naṭa, piṇḍītaka, karahāṭa, maruvaka, śalyaka, and viṣapuṣpaka [are synonyms].
Madana is sweet, bitter, hot in potency, scraping, and light.

It induces vomiting, cures abscesses, and ends catarrh and ulcers; it is parching and removes skin diseases, phlegm, abdominal distension, swelling, tumors, and wounds. (163) Rāsnā is also known as yuktarasā, rasyā, suvahā, rasanā, and rasā.

Elāparṇī, surasā, sugandhā, and likewise śreyasī, as well as rāsnā, apācinī, and tiktā, are heavy and hot; they conquer kapha and vāta, and remove swelling, dyspnea, wind-blood disorders, colic, and abdominal diseases. (164–165)

It cures cough, fever, poison, the eighty types of vāta diseases, skin spots (sidhma), and heart disease. Nākulī, surasā, nāgasugandhā, gandhanākulī, nakuleṣṭā, bhujaṃgākṣī, and sarpāṅgī are destroyers of poison.
Nākulī is astringent, bitter, pungent, and hot; it destroys the venom of snakes, lizards, scorpions, and rats, as well as fevers, worms, and ulcers.
Mācikā, prasthikā, ambaṣṭhā, ambālikā, and ambikā are likewise [described].
Mayūravidalā, Keśī, Sahasrā, and Bālamūlikā;
Mācikā is sour in taste and digestion, astringent, cooling, and light;
it cures chronic diarrhea, hemorrhaging due to pitta, and diseases of the throat caused by kapha. // 169–170 //
Tejasvinī, tejavatī, tejohvā, and likewise tejanī;
tejasvinī removes phlegm, dyspnea, cough, diseases of the mouth, and wind; it is digestive, hot, pungent, and bitter, and it stimulates the appetite and kindles the digestive fire. // 171 //
*Jyotiṣmatī* is known as *kaṭabhī*, *jyotiṣkā*, and *kaṅgunī*;
it is also called *pārāvatapadī*, *piṇyā*, *latā*, and *kakundanī*.
*Jyotiṣmatī* is pungent, bitter, laxative, and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*.
It is very hot, emaciating, and sharp; it bestows digestive fire, intellect, and memory.
(173) Kuṣṭha is also known as rogāhvaya, vāpya, pāribhavya, and utpala.
Kuṣṭha is hot, pungent, sweet, aphrodisiac, bitter, and light. (174)

It destroys wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, erysipelas, cough, leprosy, and disorders of wind and phlegm. (175) They say that *puṣkaramūla*, *pauṣkara*, and *puṣkara* are synonyms for *padmapattra* and *kāśmīra*; they declare this to be a variety of *kuṣṭha*. (176)

Pauṣkara is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys wind, phlegm, and fevers, as well as swelling, anorexia, and dyspnea, and specifically relieves pain in the flanks. Kaṭuparṇī, haimavatī, hemakṣīrī, and himāvatī [are synonyms].
Hemāhvā and pītadugdhā—its root is called coka.
Hemāhvā is purgative, bitter, a laxative, and causes nausea;
it destroys worms, itching, poisons, abdominal distension, phlegm, bile, blood disorders, and leprosy.
Śṛṅgī is known as karkaṭaśṛṅgī and kulīraviṣāṇikā;
however, ajaśṛṅgī is celebrated as cakrā and by the name karkaṭā.
Śṛṅgī is astringent, bitter, and hot; it [cures] disorders of phlegm and wind, consumption, and fever.
It removes dyspnea, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), thirst, cough, hiccups, aversion to food, and vomiting.
Kaṭphala, somavalka, kaiṭarya, kumbhikā, śrīparṇikā, kumudikā, bhadrā, and bhadravatī [are also used for this]. // 181–182 //

Kaṭphala is astringent and bitter; it destroys wind, phlegm, and fever, as well as asthma, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, throat diseases, and loss of appetite. (183) Bhārgī, bhṛgubhavā, padmā, phaṃjī, and brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā [are synonyms].

Brāhmaṇyaṅgāravallī, kharaśāka, and hañjikā—these are known as bhārgī. It is dry, pungent, bitter, appetizing, hot, digestive, and light. It stimulates the digestive fire, is astringent, and certainly destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and hemorrhaging.

Pāṣāṇabheda, aśmaghna, giribhit, bhinnayojinī, and aśmabheda are cooling, bitter, and astringent; they cleanse the bladder and alleviate swelling, cough, phlegm, asthma, chronic rhinitis, fever, and wind disorders. (185–186)

Bhedana destroys the humors (doṣas), hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary calculi, heart disease, gynecological disorders, urinary disorders (prameha), splenic enlargement, colic, and ulcers.
Dhātakī, dhātupuṣpī, tāmrapuṣpī, and kuñjarā [are synonyms]. 187.
Subhikṣā, Bahupuṣpī, and Vahnijvālā are known as synonyms for Dhātakī.
It is pungent, cooling, softening, astringent, and light;
it conquers thirst, diarrhea, bile, blood disorders, poisons, worms, and erysipelas.
Mañjiṣṭhā, vikasā, jiṅgī, samaṅgā, kālameṣikā, maṇḍūkaparṇī, bhaṇḍīrī, bhaṇḍī, and yojanavallī;
also rasāyanī, aruṇā, kālā, raktāṅgī, and raktayaṣṭikā. (190–191)

Bhaṇḍītakī, gambhīrī, mañjūṣā, and vastrarañjinī—known as mañjiṣṭhā—are sweet, bitter, and astringent; they improve the voice and complexion. They are heavy and hot, and they cure poison, phlegm, swelling, diseases of the female reproductive tract, and pains of the eyes and ears.
It cures dysentery with blood, leprosy, hemorrhaging, erysipelas, ulcers, and urinary disorders.
Kusumbha is also known as Vahniśikha and Vastrarañjaka.
Kusumbha increases Vāta and removes difficult urination (kṛcchra), blood-bile (raktapitta), and Kapha. (193–194)
Lākṣā, palaṅkaṣā, alaktaka, yāva, vṛkṣāmaya, and jatū are synonyms for lac.
Lac improves the complexion; it is cooling, strengthening, unctuous, astringent, and light.
It is not hot and subdues phlegm, bile, blood disorders, hiccups, cough, and fever.

It removes wounds, chest injuries, erysipelas, worms, and leprosy. Alaktaka possesses similar qualities, and it is especially effective in destroying facial freckles. Haridrā, kāñcanī, pītā, niśākhyā, and varavarṇinī are synonyms for turmeric.
Kṛmighnī, haladī, yoṣitpriyā, and haṭṭavilāsinī are synonyms for haridrā (turmeric). It is pungent, bitter, dry, and hot; it subdues kapha and pitta.
It improves the complexion and cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, blood disorders, swelling, anemia, and wounds.
*Dārvī*, *bhedā*, *āmragandhā*, *surabhī*, *dāru*, and *dāru* [are synonyms for *daruharidrā*].
*Karpūrā*, *padmapattrā*, *surīmat*, and *suratārakā* [are synonyms for *kālīyaka*].
*Āmragandhi* is *haridrā*; it is considered cold and increases wind (*vāta*).
It removes bile, is sweet and bitter, and destroys all types of itching.
The bulbous root of *araṇyahaladī* destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and gout (*vātāsra*).
*Dārvī*, *dāruharidrā*, *parjanyā*, and *parjanī* are synonyms [for the same plant].
Kaṭaṅkaṭerī, when yellow, is called pacampacā;
it is also termed kālīyaka as well as kāleyaka.
Furthermore, it is known as pītadru, haridrā, pītadāru, and pītaka.
Dārvī possesses the qualities of niśā, but it specifically cures diseases of the eyes, ears, and mouth.
When milk equal in volume to a decoction of dārvī is boiled down until it becomes thick—reduced to one-fourth—it is then called rasāñjana; this is supremely beneficial for the eyes. (204–205)
Rasāñjana, tārkṣyaśaila, rasagarbha, and tārkṣyajam—these are synonyms for rasāñjana.
Rasāñjana is pungent, cures disorders of phlegm and poison, and alleviates eye diseases;
it is hot, an elixir (rasāyana), bitter, incising, and removes defects of wounds. 206–207.
Avalguja is known as vākucī, somarājī, suparṇikā, śaśilekhā, kṛṣṇaphalā, somā, and pūtiphalī;
it is also celebrated as somavallī, kālameṣī, and kuṣṭhaghnī. // 208 //

Vākucī is sweet and bitter, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and a rejuvenative (rasāyana). It causes constipation, increases the appetite, is palatable, laxative, and alleviates phlegm (śleṣman) and blood-bile (asrapitta).
It is dry, pleasing to the heart, and cures asthma, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), fever, and worms.

Its fruit is pungent, increases pitta, and alleviates skin diseases (kuṣṭha), kapha, and vāta; it is beneficial for the hair, good for the skin, and cures worms, asthma, cough, swelling, indigestion, and anemia. Cakramarda, prapunnāṭī, dadrughna, and meṣalocana are synonyms.
Padmāṭa is known as eḍagaja, cakrī, and also as puṃnāṭa.
Cakramarda is light, sweet, and dry; it subdues pitta and vāta.
It is pleasing to the heart and cooling, and it removes kapha, asthma, leprosy, ringworm, and worms.
That fruit is hot; it destroys leprosy, itching, ringworm, poisons, and wind disorders.
It is known to be pungent and is a destroyer of abdominal tumors, cough, worms, and asthma.
Viṣā, ativiṣā, viśvā, śṛṅgī, prativiṣā, and aruṇā [are synonyms for ativiṣā].

Śuklakandā, upaviṣā, bhaṅgurā, and ghuṇavallabhā are poisonous, hot, pungent, and bitter; they are digestive stimulants and appetizers, and they remove phlegm, bile, diarrhea, worms, poison, cough, vomiting, and parasites. // 215-216 //
Lodhra, tilva, tirīṭa, śāvara, and likewise gālava;
the second is paṭṭikālodhra, kramuka, sthūlavalkala,
jīrṇapattra, bṛhatpattra, paṭṭī, and lākṣāprasādana.
Lodhra is astringent, light, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and subdues kapha and pitta;
it is astringent and removes bleeding disorders, blood-bile, fever, diarrhea, and swelling.
(219) Laśuna is known as rasona, ugragandha, and mahauṣadha.
It is called *ariṣṭa*, *mlecchakanda*, *yavaneṣṭa*, and *rasonaka*.
When Vainateya carried away the nectar (*amṛta*) from the best of the gods, a drop fell from it at that time, and it became the *rasona* on the earth. // 220–221 //
Endowed with five tastes and devoid of the sour taste, it is therefore called *rasona* by those who know the qualities of substances. Furthermore,
there is one that is bitter in its roots and resides in its leaves.
The stalk is declared to be astringent; the tip of the stalk is known to be salty;
and the seed is said by those who know its qualities to have a sweet taste.
Garlic is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, hot, digestive, and laxative.
In taste and post-digestive effect, it is considered pungent, sharp, and sweet.
It heals fractures, is beneficial for the throat, heavy, and increases bile and blood.
It bestows strength and complexion, is conducive to intelligence, beneficial for the eyes, and acts as a rejuvenative tonic (rasāyana).
It destroys heart disease, chronic fever, abdominal colic, constipation, abdominal tumors, anorexia, cough, edema,
hemorrhoids, skin diseases, loss of digestive fire, parasites, disorders of wind, dyspnea, and phlegm. Wine, meat, and sour substances are likewise beneficial for those who consume garlic.
A man who eats garlic should avoid these things continuously: physical exertion, exposure to the sun, anger, excessive water, milk, molasses, and onions—
which are favored by the Yavanas, foul-smelling, and corrupting to the mouth.
Onions (palāṇḍu) should be known by the wise as being similar in properties to garlic (rasona).
They are sweet in taste and digestion, non-heating in potency, increase phlegm (kapha), and do not excessively increase bile (pitta).
They exclusively subdue wind (vāta), bestow strength and virility, and are heavy [to digest]. (228–229)
Bhallātaka is said to have three names: aruṣka, aruṣkara, and agnika;
likewise, it is called agnimukhī, bhallī, vīravṛkṣa, and śophakṛt.
The ripe fruit of the bhallātaka is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect (vipāka), and is light.
It is astringent, digestive, unctuous, sharp, hot, scarifying, and disintegrating;

it promotes intelligence, stimulates the digestive fire, and destroys phlegm, wind, wounds, abdominal enlargements, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, tumors, edema, flatulence, fever, and worms. (231–232)
Its marrow is sweet, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and subdues wind and bile.
The stalk of the *āruṣkara* is sweet, pacifies bile, promotes hair growth, and stimulates the digestive fire.
*Bhallātaka* is astringent, hot, spermatogenic, sweet, and light.

It destroys abdominal enlargement caused by wind and phlegm, flatulence, leprosy, hemorrhoids, diseases of the digestive tract, tumors, fever, vitiligo, weak digestion, worms, and ulcers. (234) Bhaṅgā, gañjā, mātulānī, mādinī, vijayā, and jayā are synonyms for hemp. (235)
Bhaṅgā removes phlegm, is bitter, constipating, digestive, and light;
it is sharp, hot, increases bile, and augments delusion, slowness of speech, and the digestive fire.
Tilabheda is known as khasatila and also as khākhasa.
The bark produced from the Khākhasa fruit is cooling and light;
it is astringent, bitter, and astringent-tasting (kaṣāya), generates wind (vāta), and removes phlegm and cough.
It dries up the bodily tissues (dhātus), is parching, causes intoxication, and increases speech.
It causes repeated delusion, is pleasant to the taste, and destroys virility through its use.
(239) Khasaphala-kṣīra is said to be Āphūka and Mahiphenaka.
Āphūka is drying, constipating, destroys phlegm, and increases wind and bile.
Likewise, it is said that they consist mostly of bark produced from the *khasa* fruit;
these are called *khasabīja*, as well as *khākhasa* and *tila*.
The *khasabījas* are strengthening (*balya*), aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), and very heavy (*guru*).
These [substances] generate phlegm and pacify the wind (vāta).
Saindhava—also known as śītaśiva and māṇimantha—is produced from the Sindhu region.
Saindhava salt is sweet, digestive-stimulant, carminative, and light.
It is unctuous, palatable, cooling, aphrodisiac, subtle, beneficial for the eyes, and removes the three doṣas.
(243) That which is called Śākambharīya, as well as Guḍākhya and Raumaka, have been described.
(244) Guḍākhya is light, subdues Vāta, is extremely hot, is a purgative, and increases Pitta.
It is sharp, hot, subtle, obstructive to the channels, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka).
That which is sea salt (sāmudra), also known as akṣība and vaśira,
is born from the ocean, produced by the sea, and originates from the salt-water ocean.
Sea salt is sweet in its post-digestive effect, slightly bitter, sweet, and heavy;
it is not excessively hot, stimulates the digestive fire, is purgative, contains milk, and does not cause a burning sensation.
It increases phlegm, subdues wind, is sharp, non-dry, and not excessively cold. (247)

Viḍa, pāka, kṛtaka, as well as drāviḍa and āsura—among these, viḍa is alkaline and promotes the downward and upward movement of phlegm and wind; that is to say, it causes phlegm to move upward and wind to move downward. // 248

Sauvarcala salt is digestive, light, sharp, hot, dry, appetizing, and pervasive; it removes obstructions, flatulence, constipation, heart disease, heaviness, and colic. It is known as rucaka and manthapāka. (249)
Rucaka is appetizing, laxative, a superior digestive stimulant and carminative;
it is very unctuous, subdues Vāta, slightly increases Pitta, is clear, light, promotes pure eructation, is subtle, and conquers constipation, abdominal distension, and colic. (250–251)
Audbhida salt is that which is produced from the earth itself;
it is alkaline, heavy, pungent, unctuous, cooling, and destroys wind disorders.
Chickpea vinegar is extremely hot, stimulates digestion, and causes the teeth to tingle.

Having salt as its secondary taste, it is appetizing and removes colic, indigestion, and constipation. Yavakṣāra, yāvaśūka, and yavāgraja are known as pākya-kṣāra (alkali produced by cooking). Svarjikā and kāpota are also considered kṣāras; they facilitate the easy passage of feces.
Suvarcikā is said by those who know the distinctions to be a variety of svarjikā.
Yavakṣāra is light, unctuous, extremely subtle, and an inflamer of the digestive fire;
it destroys colic, wind-disorders, fever, phlegm, asthma, and diseases of the throat.
It cures jaundice, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), flatulence, splenic enlargement, and heart diseases.
Svarjikā is to be known as having slightly lesser qualities than that [sajjīkṣāra], yet it removes abdominal tumors and colic.
Suvarcikā should be understood by people to possess qualities similar to those of svarjikā.
Saubhāgya, ṭaṅkaṇa, and kṣāra are said to be metal-fluxing agents (*dhātudrāvaka*).
Ṭaṅkaṇa stimulates the digestive fire, is parching, removes phlegm (*kapha*), and increases wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
Svarjikā and yāvaśūka are declared to be the two types of alkali (*kṣāradvaya*).

That [alkali] combined with ṭaṅkaṇa is declared to be the "three alkalis" (kṣāratraya). When combined, they produce the aforementioned qualities; specifically, they are supreme in removing abdominal tumors (gulma).
[The ashes of] Palāśa, Vajrī, Śikhari, Ciñcā, Arka, and sesame stalks [are used]. // 259–260 //
Barley-alkali and svarjikā—these are declared to be the eight alkalis (kṣārāṣṭaka).
These alkalis are equal to fire and are extremely effective in removing abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic.
Vinegar that has been fermented for a thousand days is called rasāmla and also śukla.
Fermented gruel (cukra) is sour, hot, an excellent stimulant of digestion and digestive catalyst;
it removes colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, āma-vāta, and kapha; it is laxative and cures vomiting, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, cardiac pain, and weak digestion.
Bhāvaprakāśa,
Section on Classes, Chapter on Camphor and Related Substances (Karpūrādivarga)
*Karpūra* (camphor) is masculine and neuter; it is also known as *sitābhra*, *himavāluka*, *ghanasāra*, *candrasaṃjña*, and by the name *hima*.
Camphor is cooling, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, scraping, and light.
Camphor is fragrant, sweet, and bitter; it destroys phlegm, bile, and poison. It eliminates thirst, bad taste in the mouth, fat, and foul odors.
Camphor is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being either processed (*pakva*) or unprocessed (*apakva*).
They say that the unripe camphor is more efficacious than the ripe.
Camphor known as *cīnāka* is considered to cause the depletion of *kapha*; it is a destroyer of leprosy, itching, and vomiting, and it possesses a bitter taste.

Mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, and sahasrabhit are said to be synonyms for kastūrikā and kastūrī; it is also known as vedhamukhyā. That which originates from Kāmarūpa is black, while the Nepalese variety is endowed with a blue color.
Kashmiri musk is known to have a tawny hue; thus, musk is said to be of three kinds.
That produced in Kamarupa is the best, that from Nepal is middling, and musk originating in the land of Kashmir is considered the lowest.
Musk (kastūrikā) is pungent, bitter, alkaline, hot, aphrodisiac, and heavy;
it removes phlegm, wind, poison, vomiting, cold, foul odor, and wasting.
Musk from the vine (latā-kastūrikā) is bitter, sweet, aphrodisiac, cooling, and light.
It is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and removes diseases of the phlegm, thirst, bladder, and mouth.

(9) The *gandhamārjāra* is indeed an aphrodisiac, subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, removes itching and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), is beneficial for the eyes, is fragrant, and dispels the odor of sweat. (10)
Śrīkhaṇḍa, candana, na-strī, bhadraśrī, tailaparṇika, gandhasāra, malayaja, and candradyuti are synonyms for sandalwood.
It is bitter in taste, yellow when rubbed, red when cut, and white in its natural state.
Sandalwood that possesses knots and hollows is said to be the best.
Sandalwood is cooling, dry, bitter, refreshing, and light;
it removes fatigue, wasting, poisons, phlegm, thirst, blood-bile, and burning sensations.

Kālīyaka is also called kālīya; it has a yellowish luster and is known as haricandana, haripriya, kālasāra, and likewise kālānusāryaka. Kālīyaka possesses red qualities and is especially effective in destroying facial freckles and blemishes.
Red sandalwood is said to be *raktacandana*, while red-bodied *kṣudracandana* is known as *tilaparṇa* and *raktasāra*; it is also considered to have coral-like fruit (*pravālaphala*).
It is red, cooling, heavy, and sweet; it removes vomiting, thirst, and blood-bile (*asrapitta*).
It is bitter, beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and removes fever, wounds, and poison.
Pataṅga, raktasāra, suraṅga, rañjana, paṭṭarañjaka, pattūra, and kucandana are likewise declared [to be similar]. 17–18.
Pataṅga is sweet and cooling; it removes pitta, kapha, wounds, and hemorrhages.
It should be understood as being like haricandana, especially in its destruction of burning sensations.
Indeed, all varieties of sandalwood are similar in their taste and other qualities.
There is indeed a distinction by scent; the former is the most excellent in its qualities.
Agallochum (aguru) is the best, as is the "metal" (loha), that which is fit for kings, and likewise that produced by yoga.
That which comes from bamboo (vaṃśika), that born of insects (kṛmija), and even that eaten by insects (kṛmijagdha) is considered ignoble (anāryaka).
Aguru is non-heavy (light), hot, pungent, beneficial for the skin, bitter, sharp, and increases pitta; it is light, cures diseases of the ears and eyes, and dispels cold, vāta, and kapha.
Black aguru possesses superior qualities and sinks in water like iron.
The oil derived from *aguru* is known to be equal to black *aguru*.
*Devadāru*, *dārubhadra*, *dāru*, and *indradāru* are synonyms; it is also called *mastadāru*, *drukilima*, *kilima*, and *surabhūruha*.
Devadāru is light, unctuous, bitter and hot, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka).

It overcomes constipation, flatulence, swelling, lassitude, drowsiness, hiccups, fever, and blood disorders; it also cures urinary disorders (prameha), chronic catarrh, phlegm, cough, itching, and wind (vāta). (25)
Sarala is the yellow tree, as well as the Surabhidāruka.
Sarala is sweet, bitter, pungent in its post-digestive effect and taste, and light.
It is known to be unctuous and hot, and it removes diseases of the ears, throat, and eyes, as well as demons.
It removes phlegm, wind, perspiration, burning sensations, cough, fainting, and wounds.
Kālānusārya, tagara, kuṭila, nahuṣa, nata, piṇḍatagara, daṇḍahastī, and barhiṇa are synonyms for it. (27–28)

The two types of *tagara* are hot; they are considered sweet, unctuous, and light, and they remove poison, epilepsy, colic, eye diseases, and the three *doṣas*. *Padmaka* has the fragrance of a lotus and is likewise known by the name *padmāhvaya*.
Padmaka is astringent, bitter, cooling, increases wind, and is light.
It cures erysipelas, burning sensations, eruptions, skin diseases, phlegm, and blood-bile; it stabilizes the fetus, improves appetite, and alleviates vomiting, ulcers, and thirst. (30–31)
Guggulu, devadhūpa, jaṭāyu, and kauśika are synonyms for it;
kumbha and ulūkhalaka are neuter; and mahiṣākṣa and palaṅkaṣa are also used.
Furthermore, mahiṣākṣa, mahānīla, kumuda, and padma are names for varieties of this substance.

The fifth is to be known as *hiraṇya*; these are the five types of *guggulu*. That which has the color of *bhṛṅgāñjana* (bee-antimony) is remembered as *mahiṣākṣa*, while the *mahānīla* is to be understood by its characteristics corresponding to its own name.
*Kumuda* resembles a white water-lily; *padma* is like a ruby (*māṇikya*);
and *hiraṇyākṣa* has the luster of gold—this is said to be the characteristic mark of the five [types of gems].
*Mahiṣākṣa* is deep blue (*mahānīla*); both of these are beneficial for lordly elephants.
For horses, Kumuda and Padma are the two others that bestow well-being and health;
for humans specifically, Kanaka is highly praised,
though Mahiṣākṣa is also occasionally considered suitable for men by some.
Guggulu is clear, bitter, hot in potency, increases pitta, and is laxative;
it is astringent and pungent, pungent in its post-digestive effect, extremely sharp, dry, and light.
It promotes the healing of fractures, is aphrodisiac, subtle, beneficial for the voice, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
It is digestive, unctuous, and strengthening;

it conquers phlegm, wind, wounds, scrofula (apacī), fat, urinary disorders, stones, wind, moisture, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), undigested toxins (āma), and flatulence, as well as pustules, glandular swellings, edema, hemorrhoids, cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), and worms. (39–40)
Due to its sweetness it pacifies Vāta, and due to its astringency it destroys Pitta;
because of its bitterness it conquers Kapha; thus Guggulu is a destroyer of all the Doṣas. It is nourishing and aphrodisiac when fresh, but very emaciating when old.

Guggulu that is unctuous, resembling gold, comparable to a ripe jambū fruit, fragrant, and slimy is said to be fresh. That which is dry, foul-smelling, and has abandoned its natural color and quality is [unwholesome].

That old guggulu should be known as being devoid of potency. One who desires its qualities and uses it for the sake of health should properly avoid sour things, pungent things, indigestion, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, exposure to the sun, alcohol, and anger.
Śrīvāsa, saralasrāva, śrīveṣṭa, and vṛkṣadhūpaka are synonyms for pine resin.
Śrīvāsa is sweet, bitter, unctuous, hot, astringent, and laxative;
it increases pitta, yet it alleviates wind, diseases of the head, eyes, and voice, as well as kapha.
It is a destroyer of demons and a remover of sweat, foul odors, lice, itching, and wounds.
*Rāla* is known as the resin of the *śāla* tree, as well as *sarjarasa*;
it is also called *devadhūpa*, *yakṣadhūpa*, and *sarvarasa*.
Rāla is cold, heavy, bitter, and astringent;
it is absorbent and removes the humors (doṣas), blood, sweat, erysipelas, fever, ulcers, and scabies.
It cures those afflicted by planetary influences, fractures, and burns from fire, and destroys colic and diarrhea. (49)
Kundurū is known as mukunda, sugandha, and also kunda.
Kundurū is sweet, bitter, sharp, beneficial for the skin, and pungent;
it removes fever, perspiration, seizures, misfortune, diseases of the mouth, and disorders of phlegm and wind.
Sihlaka is known as turuṣka because it originates from the land of the Yavanas;
it is also reckoned as kapitaila and named after the monkey (kapināmaka).
Sihlaka is pungent, sweet, unctuous, and hot; it increases semen and enhances the luster of the complexion.
It is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the throat, and removes perspiration, leprosy, fever, burning sensations, and seizures.
Jātīphala, jātikośa, and mālatīphala are its synonyms.
Jātīphala is bitter in taste, sharp, hot, appetizing, and light.
It is pungent, digestive-stimulant, constipating, beneficial for the voice, and subdues phlegm and wind.
It destroys bad taste in the mouth, as well as oral impurities, foul odors, and blackness [of the teeth].
It also cures worms, cough, vomiting, asthma, consumption, chronic catarrh, and heart disease.
The bark of the nutmeg (*jātīphala*) is called *jātīpattrī* by the best of physicians.
*Jātīpattrī* is light, sweet, pungent, and hot; it improves appetite and complexion, and removes phlegm, cough, vomiting, asthma, thirst, worms, and poison. (56–57)
Lavaṅga is known as devakusuma, śrī, and śrīprasūnaka.
Lavaṅga is pungent, bitter, light, beneficial for the eyes, and cooling. It stimulates digestion, aids digestion, improves the appetite, and destroys phlegm, bile, and blood disorders.
It quickly destroys thirst, vomiting, flatulence, and colic;
it certainly eliminates cough, dyspnea, hiccup, and consumption.
Elā, sthūlā, bahulā, pṛthvīkā, and tripuṭā are also [known by these names]. (59–60)

Bhadrailā, bṛhadelā, candrabālā, niṣkuṭi, and sthūlailā are pungent in digestion and taste; they stimulate the digestive fire and are light. They are dry and hot, and they alleviate phlegm, bile, blood disorders, itching, asthma, and thirst.
It cures nausea, poisoning, anal disorders, facial pain, headache, vomiting,
and dyspnea. Fine *upakuñcikā*, *tuttha*, *koraṅgī*, *drāviḍī*, *truṭi*,
and fine *elā* remove phlegm, asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, and dysuria.

In terms of taste, it is pungent, cooling, light, and considered to alleviate wind (vāta). Tvakpattra, varāṅga, bhṛṅga, coca, and utkaṭa are synonyms for cinnamon bark (tvac). Cinnamon bark is light, hot, pungent, sweet, bitter, and dry.
It increases pitta, destroys kapha and vāta, and cures itching, anorexia, diseases of the heart and bladder, vāta-type hemorrhoids, worms, nasal catarrh, and seminal disorders.
Its bark is sweet and has thin bark; it is likewise considered to be "wooden sugar" (dārusitā).
Dārusitā has been described as sweet and bitter, removing wind and bile; it is fragrant, increases semen, improves the complexion, and alleviates dryness of the mouth and thirst.
Pattraka, tamālapattra, and likewise pattranāmaka are its synonyms.
Pattra-ka is slightly sweet, pungent-hot, slimy, and light;
it destroys phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, nausea, loss of appetite, and chronic catarrh.
Nāgapuṣpa is known as nāga, kesaras, and nāgakesara.
Cāmpeya is called nāgakiñjalka and is also known by the name kāñcana.
Nāgapuṣpa is astringent, hot, dry, light, and a purifier of undigested matter (āma).
It destroys fever, itching, thirst, perspiration, vomiting, and nausea.
It removes foul odors, leprosy, erysipelas, phlegm, bile, and poisons.
Equal parts of cinnamon, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves constitute *trisugandhi* (the three aromatics) or *trijātaka* (the three-fold group).
When combined with *nāgakeśara*, it is called *cāturjātaka* (the four-fold group).

That [saffron] is of two types: *rocana* (yellow) and *rūkṣa* (dry). It is sharp, hot, removes foul odors from the mouth, light, increases bile and digestive fire, improves the complexion, and destroys *kapha*, *vāta*, and poisons.
*Kuṅkuma*, *ghusṛṇa*, *rakta*, and *kāśmīra* are synonyms; the yellow variety is considered superior.
Saṃkoca, piśuna, dhīra, vāhlīka, and that which is called śoṇita—
whatever saffron (kuṅkuma) is produced in the field born of the Kāśmīra region, having fine filaments, slightly red, and smelling like a lotus, that is the most excellent. (74–75)
Saffron produced in the land of Vāhlīka is known as *pāṇḍura* (white);
it possesses the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower, has fine filaments, and is considered mediocre.
Saffron from Pārasīka is said to have the scent of honey.
That which is slightly pale in color and possesses thick filaments is of inferior quality.
Saffron (kuṅkuma) is pungent, unctuous, and conquers headache, wounds, and parasites;
it is bitter, cures vomiting, improves the complexion, and removes freckles as well as the three doṣas.
Gorocanā is auspicious, venerable, and is known as Gaurī and Rocanā.
Gorocanā is cooling, bitter, improves the complexion, and bestows auspiciousness and luster.
It removes poison, misfortune, planetary afflictions, insanity, miscarriage, wounds, and hemorrhaging. (79)
Nakha, vyāghranakha, and vyāghrāyudha are names for that which produces cakras (whorls).
Nakha is also called svalpanakha and nakhī; it is known as hanu and haṭṭavilāsinī.
The substance nakha removes seizures, phlegm, wind, blood disorders, fever, and leprosy.

It is light, hot, aphrodisiac, improves the complexion, is sweet, cures wounds and poison, removes misfortune, facial discoloration, and foul odor; it is pungent in both its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and taste (rasa). 82.
Bāla, hrīvera, barhiṣṭha, udīcya, and keśāmbu are its synonyms.
Bālaka is cooling, dry, light, and an appetizer and digestive;
it conquers nausea, anorexia, erysipelas, heart disease, and diarrhea.
Vīraṇa, vīrataru, vīra, and bahumūlaka are synonyms for it.
Vīraṇa is digestive, cooling, antiemetic, light for the heart, and bitter;
it is astringent, febrifuge, overcomes vertigo and intoxication, and removes phlegm and bile.
It cures thirst, blood disorders, poisons, erysipelas, dysuria, burning sensations, and wounds.
The root of *vīraṇa* is known as *uśīra*, *nalada*, *amṛṇāla*, *sevya*, and also *samagandhika*.
(86) *Uśīra* is digestive, cooling, astringent, light, and bitter. (87)
It is sweet, removes fever, alleviates vomiting and diarrhea, and subdues *kapha* and *pitta*.
It cures thirst, poisoning, erysipelas (*vīsarpa*), burning sensations, dysuria, and wounds.
(88) *Jaṭāmāṃsī*, *bhūtajaṭā*, *jaṭilā*, and *tapasvinī* [are its synonyms].
Māṃsī is bitter and astringent; it promotes intelligence and bestows luster and strength.

It is sweet, cooling, and alleviates the three doṣas, as well as hemorrhaging, burning sensations, erysipelas, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). (89) Śaileya, śilāpuṣpa, vṛddha, and kālānusāryaka are synonyms. (90)

Śaileya is cooling, pleasing to the heart, light, and it removes phlegm and bile; it cures itching, skin diseases, urinary stones, burning sensations, and poisons, and it alleviates hemorrhoids and bleeding from the rectum.
Mustaka is not feminine; musta is used in all three genders and is also known by the name vārida.
Kuruvinda is enumerated as another [variety], as well as kroḍakaseruka,
bhadramusta, gundrā, and likewise nāgaramustaka.
Musta is pungent, cooling, astringent, bitter, digestive, and carminative.
Astringent, it removes phlegm, bile, blood, thirst, fever, anorexia, and parasites.
Musta grown in marshy regions is highly praised;
among those, the sages have declared Nagara-musta to be the best. (94)
Karcūra, Vedhamukhya, Drāviḍa, Kalpaka, and Śaṭī are synonyms for Karcūra.
Karcūra is digestive, appetizing, pungent, and bitter;
it is fragrant, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cures skin diseases, hemorrhoids, ulcers, and cough.
Hot and light, it cures dyspnea, abdominal tumors, disorders of wind and phlegm, and worms.
(96) Murā, Gandhakuṭī, Daityā, Surabhi, and Śālaparṇikā are synonyms for Murā.
(97) Murā is bitter, cooling, sweet, and light; it alleviates pitta and vāta.
Śaṭhī destroys fever, blood disorders, spirits, and Rākṣasas, and it cures skin diseases and cough.
It is known as palāśī, ṣaḍgranthā, suvratā, gandhamūlikā, gāndhārikā, gandhavadhū, vadhū, and palāśikā. (98–99)
Gandhapalāśī is astringent, absorbent, and light;
it is bitter, sharp, and pungent, slightly warm, and destroys impurities of the mouth.
It cures swelling, cough, wounds, asthma, colic, sidhma skin disease, and seizures. (100)
Priyaṅgu is known as phalinī, kāntā, latā, and mahilāhvayā;
it is also called gundrā, gandhaphalā, śyāmā, and viṣvaksenāṅganāpriyā.
Priyaṅgu is cooling, bitter, astringent, and removes wind and bile.
Gandhapriyaṅgu likewise removes excessive hemorrhaging, foul odor, perspiration, burning sensations, and fever; it destroys abdominal tumors, thirst, poison, and delusion.
Its fruit is sweet, dry, astringent, cooling, and heavy.
It relieves constipation and flatulence, increases strength, is astringent, and conquers *kapha* and *pitta*.
Reṇukā, rājaputrī, nandinī, kapilā, dvijā, bhasmagandhā, pāṇḍuputrī, kauntī, and hareṇukā are known as synonyms for this plant. (104–105)

Reṇukā is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), bitter, non-hot, pungent, and light; it increases bile, stimulates digestion, improves the intellect, promotes digestion, and causes abortion; it produces phlegm and wind, and it removes thirst, itching, poison, and burning sensations. (106)
Granthiparṇa, granthika, kākapuccha, gucchaka, nīlapuṣpa, sugandha, and tailaparṇaka are thus described.
Granthiparṇa is bitter and sharp, pungent and hot, digestive, and light.
It destroys phlegm, wind, poison, asthma, itching, and foul odors.
Sthauṇeyaka, barhibarha, śukabarha, kukkura, śīrṇaromaśuka, śukapuṣpa, and śukacchada [are synonyms]. // 108–109 //

Sthauṇeyaka is pungent, sweet, and bitter; it is unctuous and alleviates the three doṣas. It promotes intelligence and semen, stimulates the appetite, destroys demons, and conquers fever and parasites. It cures skin diseases, hemorrhagic disorders, thirst, burning sensations, foul odors, moles, and freckles.
It is known as niśācara, dhanahara, kitava, and gaṇahāsa;
it is called coraka, śaṅkita, caṇḍa, duṣpattra, kṣemaka, and ripu;
it is rocaka, madhura, tikta, and kaṭu; it is pungent in digestion, light, and beneficial. (112)

Tālīśa is sharp, pleasant to the heart, and cooling; it destroys skin diseases, itching, phlegm, and wind disorders, as well as demons, lack of wealth, sweat, fat, blood, fever, foul odors, poisons, and wounds.
It is said to be rich in leaves, and is also known as dhātrīpattra.
Tālīśa is light, sharp, and hot; it destroys asthma, cough, phlegm, and wind disorders, as well as anorexia, abdominal tumors (gulma), āma, weak digestive fire, and wasting diseases.
Kaṅkola is said to be kola, and it is also known as kośaphala. (114–115)
Kaṅkola is light, sharp, hot, bitter, pleasing to the heart, and provides relish;
it removes foul breath, heart disease, disorders of phlegm and wind, and blindness.
Gandhakokilā is unctuous, hot, bitter, fragrant, and removes phlegm.
Gandhamālatī should be known as being similar to Gandhakokilā. Lāmajjaka, sunāla, amṛṇāla, lava, laghu, iṣṭakāpathaka, savya, nalada, and vidārataka are synonyms [for mṛṇāla]. 117–118.
Lāmajjaka is cooling, bitter, light, and it conquers the three *doṣas*,
blood disorders, skin diseases, excessive sweating, dysuria, burning sensations, and diseases of *pitta* and blood. Elavāluka, aileyaka, sugandhi, and harivāluka [are also known by these names].
Ailavāluka, elālu, and kapittha are said to be synonyms for pattra.
Elālu is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), astringent, cooling, and light;
it destroys itching, ulcers, vomiting, thirst, cough, loss of appetite, and heart disease.
[These cure] phlegm, poison, bile, blood disorders, leprosy, urinary ailments, and worms;
as well as *kuṭannaṭa*, *dāsapura*, *bāleya*, *paripelava*, *plava*, *gopura*, *gonarda*, *kaivartī*, and *mustaka*. (121–122)
Vitunnaka has thin petals like mustā and is white like a parrot.
Vitunnaka is cooling, bitter, astringent, pungent, and bestows luster;
it destroys phlegm, bile, blood disorders, erysipelas, leprosy, itching, and poisons. (123–124)
*Spṛkkā*, *asṛg*, *brāhmaṇa*, *deva*, *marunmālā*, *latā*, *laghu*,
*samudrāntā*, *vadhū*, *koṭivarṣā*, and also *laṅkopikā*— these are synonyms for *spṛkkā*.
*Spṛkkā* is sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, bitter, and a remover of all the bodily humors (*doṣa*).
It removes leprosy, itching, poison, perspiration, burning sensations, lack of luster, fever, and blood disorders.
Parpaṭī, rañjanī, kṛṣṇā, jatukā, jananī, janī, jatukṛṣṇā, agnisaṃsparśā, jatukṛt, and cakravartinī are synonyms. (126–127)
Parpaṭī is astringent, bitter, cooling, complexion-enhancing, and light;
it removes poison and wounds, and cures itching, kapha, pitta, blood disorders, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Nalikā, vidrumalatā, kapotacaraṇā, and naṭī [are synonyms].

Dhamanī, añjanakeśī, nirmedhyā, suṣirā, and nalī—also known as nalikā, śītalā, and laghvī—are beneficial for the eyes and remove kapha and pitta. They cure dysuria, urinary stones, vāta disorders, thirst, hemorrhaging, skin diseases, itching, and fever. (129–130)
Prapauṇḍarīka, pauṇḍarya, cakṣuṣya, and pauṇḍarīyaka—pauṇḍarya is sweet, bitter, astringent, aphrodisiac, and cooling;
it is beneficial for the eyes, sweet in its post-digestive effect, improves the complexion, and subdues pitta and kapha. (131)
Bhāvaprakāśa,
Section on Classes,
Class beginning with Guḍūcī (Guḍūcyādivarga)
Then the proud Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas and ruler of Laṅkā,
afflicted by passion, forcibly abducted Sītā, the wife of Rāma. Thereupon, the powerful Rāma [confronted] that enemy who had carried off his wife.
Carried away by the monkey army, he struck him down at the head of the battle.
When that enemy of the gods, Rāvaṇa, who was arrogant in his strength,
was slain, the thousand-eyed king of the gods was highly pleased with Rāghava.
There, those monkeys who had been slain by the rākṣasas in battle,
Indra restored to life by sprinkling them with showers of nectar.
Then, in those places where [the nectar] had fallen from the bodies of the monkeys—
Drops of nectar fell [from the sky], and from them *guḍūcī* was born.
*Guḍūcī*, *madhuparṇī*, *amṛtā*, *amṛtavallarī*, *chinnā*, *chinnaruhā*, *chinnodbhavā*, and *vatsādanī* are its names.
Jīvantī, tantrikā, somā, somavallī, kuṇḍalī,
cakralakṣaṇikā, dhīrā, viśalyā, rasāyanī, candrahāsā, vayaḥsthā, maṇḍalī, and devanirmitā.

Guḍūcī is bitter, pungent, and a rejuvenator (rasāyana); it is astringent in its post-digestive effect, constipating, astringent, hot, light, strengthening, and a stimulator of the digestive fire. It cures the three doṣas, indigestion, thirst, burning sensations, urinary disorders (meha), cough, and jaundice.
It removes jaundice, skin diseases, wind-blood disorders, fever, worms, and parasites;
it also cures urinary disorders, asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, dysuria, heart disease, and wind ailments.
(10) Tāmbūlavallī, tāmbūlī, nāginī, and nāgavallarī are synonyms for betel vine.
Betel leaf is clarifying, appetizing, sharp, hot, astringent, and laxative.
It is subjugating, bitter, pungent, alkaline, light, and causes an increase in blood and bile (raktapitta).
It is strengthening and removes phlegm, foul breath, impurities, wind disorders, and fatigue. (11–12)
Bilva, śāṇḍilya, and śailūṣa are also known as mālūra and śrīphala.
Śrīphala is astringent, bitter, constipating, dry, and it stimulates the digestive fire and increases pitta;
it alleviates vāta and kapha, is strengthening, light, hot, and a digestive aid. // 13 //
Gāmbhārī, bhadraparṇī, śrīparṇī, madhuparṇikā, kāśmīrī, kāśmarī, hīrā, kāśmaryaḥ, and pītarohiṇī;
also kṛṣṇavṛntā, madhurasā, and mahākusumikā.

Kāśmarī is astringent, bitter, hot in potency, sweet, and heavy. It stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, is beneficial for the intellect, acts as a laxative, and overcomes vertigo and wasting. It removes the humors (doṣas), thirst, anemia, colic, hemorrhoids, poison, burning sensations, and fever.
Its fruit is nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, beneficial for the hair, and an elixir;
it cures disorders of wind and bile, thirst, blood depletion, and urinary obstruction.
It is sweet in its post-digestive effect, cooling, unctuous, slightly astringent-acidic, and promotes purification.
It destroys burning sensations, thirst, vāta, blood disorders, pitta, wounds, and consumption.
Pāṭali is known as pāṭalā, amoghā, madhudūtī, phaleruhā, kṛṣṇavṛntā, kuberākṣī, kālasthālī, and alivallabhā. (18–19)
Tāmrapuṣpī is also mentioned; another variety is white Pāṭalā.
Muṣkaka, Mokṣaka, Ghaṇṭāpāṭali, and Kāṣṭhapāṭalā are synonyms.
Pāṭalā is astringent and bitter, not hot in potency, and it removes the three doṣas.
It removes loss of appetite, dyspnea, swelling, hemorrhage, vomiting, hiccup, and thirst.
The flower is astringent, sweet, cooling, beneficial for the heart, and subdues kapha and blood disorders.
The fruit cures pitta-type diarrhea, is beneficial for the throat, and removes hiccup and bleeding disorders.
Agnimantha is also known as Jaya, Śrīparṇī, Gaṇikārikā,
Jayā, Jayantī, Tarkārī, Nādeyī, and Vaijayantikā. Agnimantha cures swelling, is hot in potency, and removes phlegm and wind.
Śyonāka is pungent, bitter, astringent, and sweet; it stimulates the digestive fire and is desiccant.
Naṭa, kaṭvaṅga, ṭuṇṭuka, maṇḍūkaparṇa, pattrorṇa, śukanāsa, and kuṭannaṭa are synonyms for it.

Dīrghavṛnta, aralu, pṛthuśimba, kaṭaṃbhara, and śyonāka are digestive stimulants; they are pungent in digestion, astringent, and cold. They are absorbent, bitter, and destroy wind, phlegm, bile, and cough. (26)
The young fruit of the *ṭuṇṭuka* is dry and alleviates wind and phlegm (27).
It is pleasing to the heart, astringent, sweet, appetizing, light, and digestive.
When mature, it cures abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and worms; it is heavy and aggravates wind (28).
Śrīphala, sarvatobhadra, pāṭalā, gaṇikārikā,
and śyonāka— these five together are considered the great *pañcamūla*.
The great *pañcamūla* is bitter and astringent, and it subdues *kapha* and *vāta*.
Śāliparṇī is sweet, cures dyspnea and cough, is hot, light, and stimulates the digestive fire.
It is also known as sthirā, saumyā, triparṇī, pīvarī, guhā, vidārigandhā, dīrghāṅgī, dīrghapattrā, and aṃśumatī. (30–31)

Śāliparṇī is heavy; it conquers vomiting, fever, dyspnea, and diarrhea. It removes consumption and the three doṣas, is described as nourishing, and is an elixir (rasāyana). It is bitter, an antidote to poison, sweet, and it dispels chest wounds, cough, and worms.
Pṛśniparṇī, pṛthakparṇī, citraparṇī, and ahiparṇī;
kroṣṭuvinnā, siṃhapucchī, kalaśī, dhāvanī, and guhā are synonyms for pṛśniparṇī.
Pṛśniparṇī destroys the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, hot, sweet, and laxative.
It destroys burning fever, dyspnea, blood-dysentery, thirst, and vomiting.
Vārttākī, kṣudrabhaṇṭākī, mahatī, bṛhatī, kulī, hiṅgulī, rāṣṭrikā, siṃhī, mahoṣṭrī, and duṣpradharṣiṇī [are synonyms]. // 35–36 //

Bṛhatī is constipating, beneficial for the heart, digestive, and increases phlegm and wind. It destroys pungency, bitterness, bad taste in the mouth, foul odors, and loss of appetite. Being hot in potency, it conquers skin diseases, fever, asthma, colic, cough, and weak digestion. (37)
Kaṇṭakārī, duḥsparśā, kṣudrā, vyāghrī,
nidigdhikā, kaṇṭālikā, kaṇṭakinī, dhāvanī, bṛhatī, śvetā, kṣudrā, candrahāsā, lakṣmaṇā, and kṣetradūtikā.

Garbhadā, candramā, candrī, candrapuṣpā, and priyaṃkarī—these are synonyms for kaṇṭakārī. It is slightly bitter, pungent, digestive, and light; it is dry, hot, and promotes digestion. It cures cough, asthma, fever, phlegm, and wind disorders.
It destroys coryza, pain in the flanks, worms, and heart diseases (41).
The fruit of these two is pungent in taste and pungent in its post-digestive effect;
it purges the semen, is a laxative, bitter, increases bile and digestive fire, and is light.
It destroys phlegm, wind, itching, cough, fat, worms, and fever.
Similarly, the small white variety (sitā-kṣudrā) is said to have these properties, but it is especially an inducer of conception.
Gokṣura is also known as kṣuraka, trikaṇṭa, and svādukaṇṭaka.
Gokanṭaka, gokṣuraka, and vanaśṛṅgāṭa; palankaṣā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and likewise ikṣugandhikā are synonyms for gokṣura.
Gokṣura is cooling, sweet, strength-promoting, and a purifier of the bladder.
It is sweet, digestive, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and removes urinary calculi;
it cures urinary disorders, asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, dysuria, heart disease, and wind disorders.
(46) Śāliparṇī, Pṛśniparṇī, Vārttākī, and Kaṇṭakārikā [possess these qualities].
Gokṣura together with these five constitutes the *kaniṣṭha-pañcamūla* (the smallest pentad of roots).
This *pañcamūla* is light, sweet, strengthening, and subdues pitta and vāta;
it is not excessively hot, is nourishing, constipating, and cures fever, dyspnea, and urinary calculi.
The "Ten Roots" (daśamūla) is said to consist of both sets of five roots.
Daśamūla destroys the three doṣas and removes dyspnea, cough, headache, drowsiness, swelling, fever, abdominal distension, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite. (49)
Jīvantī, jīvanī, jīvā, jīvanīyā, madhusravā, the one with auspicious names, the best of greens, and the milky plant (payasvinī).
Jīvantī is cooling, sweet, unctuous, and removes the three doṣas.
Mudgaparṇī is an elixir, strength-promoting, beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and light. It is also called Kākaparṇī, Sūryaparṇī, Alpikā, Sahā, Kākamudgā, and Mārjāragandhikā. (51–52)
Mudgaparṇī is cooling, dry, bitter, and sweet;
it increases semen, is beneficial for the eyes, cures wounds and swelling, is astringent, and alleviates fever and burning sensations.
It removes the three doṣas, is light, and overcomes disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, and diarrhea. (53–54)
